title: Strict Conditions: Siempre y Cuando and More

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know three ways to make a strict condition: *con tal de que* from B1 Unit 21, *siempre que* from B2 Unit 7 and *a condición de que* from B2 Unit 9. They say that the main clause is true only if the condition is met, and the verb after them is in the subjunctive: the present subjunctive after a present or future verb, the imperfect subjunctive after a conditional or past verb (*Dijeron que firmarían siempre que les diéramos más tiempo*). The subjunctive is there because you are naming a requirement, not stating a fact. This lesson adds two more phrases. *Siempre y cuando* is *siempre que* with more weight, and it only ever means "provided that", never "whenever". *Con la condición de que* is a longer *a condición de que*.

sections.title: Strict conditions
rows: con la condición de que + subjunctive

items.spanish: Te presto el coche siempre y cuando lo devuelvas antes de las seis.
items.english: I will lend you the car as long as you bring it back before six.

items.spanish: El dueño devolverá la fianza siempre y cuando dejemos el apartamento limpio.
items.english: The owner will return the deposit as long as we leave the flat clean.

items.spanish: Firmaremos el contrato con la condición de que nos den más tiempo.
items.english: We will sign the contract on the condition that they give us more time.

items.spanish: Dijeron que aceptarían siempre y cuando bajáramos el precio.
items.english: They said they would accept as long as we lowered the price.

sections.content: Compare a plain *si* with a strict condition. You know *si* + present from B1 Unit 8, and *Te presto el coche si me avisas* just says what will happen. *Te presto el coche siempre y cuando me avises* makes your warning a requirement. After all these phrases, keep the subjunctive: say *siempre y cuando lleguen a tiempo*, not *siempre y cuando llegan* or *llegarán*, even when the main verb is in the future.
